title: Long Mott (Dow / X-energy): (PUBLIC) DRAFT SE Chapter 2 - LMGS CPA - Site Characteristics [['Safety Evaluation']]

documents.text:
OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


THIS NRC STAFF DRAFT SE HAS BEEN PREPARED AND IS BEING RELEASED TO
SUPPORT INTERACTIONS WITH THE ACRS. THIS DRAFT SE HAS NOT BEEN SUBJECT
TO FULL NRC MANAGEMENT AND LEGAL REVIEWS AND APPROVALS, AND ITS
CONTENTS SHOULD NOT BE INTERPRETED AS OFFICIAL AGENCY POSITIONS.

2     SITE CHARACTERISTICS


This chapter of the safety evaluation (SE) describes the NRC staff’s review and evaluation of
the Long Mott Generating Station (LMGS) preliminary safety analysis report (PSAR) chapter 2,
“Site Characteristics,” which contains preliminary information on site characteristics. The
purpose of evaluating the site characteristics for a proposed reactor facility is to determine
whether the site selected is suitable to construct and operate the proposed facility. Site
characteristics evaluated include geography and demography; nearby industrial, transportation,
and military facilities; meteorology; hydrology; and geology, seismology, and geotechnical
engineering.
2.1       Geography and Demography
PSAR section 2.1 discusses site geography and demography and is divided into three
subsections:
   • Site Location and Description (Section 2.1.1)
   • Exclusion Area Authority and Control (Section 2.1.2)
   • Population Distribution (Section 2.1.3)


The applicable regulatory requirements related to geography and demography are as follows:

      •    10 CFR 50.34(a)(1)(ii), “Contents of Application”;
      •    10 CFR 100.3, “Definitions”;
      •    10 CFR 100.21, “Non-Seismic Siting Criteria,” paragraphs (a), (b), and (h)

The applicable guidance for the evaluation of geography and demography is:

      •    DANU-ISG-2022-02, “Chapter 2, 'Site Information'” March 2024 (ML23277A140)
      •    Regulatory Guide 4.7, “General Site Suitability Criteria for Nuclear Power Reactors,”
           Revision 4 (ML23348A082)
    2.1.1    Site

2.1.1.1 Technical Evaluation
The NRC staff evaluated the sufficiency of the PSAR information describing the geography of
the site using the guidance and acceptance criteria from DANU-ISG-2022-02. The NRC staff
referenced Google Maps and PSAR figures 2.1-3 and 2.1.2-1 to verify that the center point of
the project area falls within the proposed site. The NRC staff also referenced Google Maps to
independently verify the distances and directions specified in the PSAR to area boundaries,
roads, railways, waterways, and other significant features surrounding the proposed site. A
summary of the information provided in the PSAR that was verified by the NRC staff to
determine the acceptability of the description of the site is below.

                                                                                                   1

PSAR section 2.1.1.2 provides the coordinates of the center point of the project area. The site is
nearly level to gently sloping coastal lowland, a typical landform developed from marine
sediment deposits.
PSAR section 2.1.1.1 states that the proposed site for the LMGS is located in a coastal prairie
of the Guadalupe River Delta in Calhoun County, Texas. The proposed facility and its
supporting infrastructure will be located on an area of approximately 1,537 acres on land owned
by The Dow Chemical Company (Dow) through its subsidiary Dow Hydrocarbons & Resources,
LLC. The proposed site is approximately 22 miles (mi) southeast of the City of Victoria, Texas
and approximately 60 mi north-northeast of the City of Corpus Christi, Texas. Eleven
municipalities exist within 20 mi of the proposed site. The City of Seadrift is the closest
municipality. The City of Port Lavaca is the largest community near the proposed site. PSAR
figure 2.1-2 shows the airports, roads, and railroads within 50 mi of the proposed site. PSAR
figure 2.1-3 shows that the proposed site can be accessed via Texas State Highways 185 (TX-
185) and TX-35, and US Route 87. A railyard and a spur connect the site to the Union Pacific
Railroad connecting Bloomington and Long Mott.
PSAR section 2.1.1 states that the proposed site is adjacent to Dow Chemical Seadrift Industrial
railyard. As stated in PSAR section 2.2.2.6 and shown in PSAR figure 2.2-2, the proposed site
is located approximately 2.3 mi east of the Victoria Barge Canal. This canal connects the Port of
Victoria with the Gulf Intra-coastal Waterway. Although the proposed facility will not use the
canal for cooling the reactors, more than 400 barges use this canal annually to transport
hazardous chemicals.
2.1.1.2 Conclusion
Based on the above, the NRC staff finds that PSAR section 2.1.1 and associated figures
provide sufficient information to locate the proposed site. In addition, the NRC staff finds that the
description of the proposed site is sufficiently detailed. In addition, the NRC staff finds that the
description of the proposed site contains sufficient information to identify the types and locations
of natural and human-made features and potential hazards on or near the site and the local,
State, and Federal jurisdictions associated with the site and its surrounding area.
  2.1.2   Exclusion Area Authority and Control

2.1.2.1 Technical Evaluation
The NRC staff evaluated the sufficiency of the PSAR information provided on authority and
control of the exclusion area of the proposed facility. The NRC staff reviewed the PSAR to
identify the exclusion area boundary (EAB) and to identify the operator of the LMGS and the
entity with authority on lands within the EAB. The NRC staff further reviewed the PSAR to
identify public roads, rail roads, and waterways traversing the EAB and commercial activities
within the EAB. A summary of the information provided in the PSAR that was evaluated by the
NRC staff to determine the acceptability of the authority and control of the EAB is below.
PSAR sections 2.1.1.1, 2.1.1.3, and 2.1.2 state that the exclusion area boundary (EAB) is
0.25 mi or 1,312 ft (400 m or 0.4 km) from the radiological release envelope of the proposed
facility. PSAR section 2.1.2 also states that the radiological release envelope is a rectangular
area circumscribing the reactor building (RB), fuel handling building (FHB), and helium service
facility (HSF). The low population zone (LPZ) of the proposed facility coincides with the EAB.


                                                                                                   2
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                     OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


PSAR figures 1.1-3 and 2.1.2-1 show that there are no public roads, railroads, or waterways
within the EAB. PSAR section 2.1.2 also states that access to the proposed site is controlled,
and appropriate measures will be taken to prevent any pedestrian and vehicular intrusion into
the EAB. PSAR section 2.1.2 further states that LME has selected a subsidiary of NextEra
Energy Resources, LLC (NEER) to be the operator of LMGS and the operator will be
responsible for controlling all activities within the EAB. Additionally, there are no residents within
the EAB.
PSAR section 2.1.2.2 states that all recreational and hunting activities in addition to any
agricultural use of the land within the owner-controlled area and the EAB are prohibited and will
be controlled by the facility operator. PSAR section 2.1.2.2 also states that there are a few water
bodies nearby, which are industrial basins, as shown in PSAR figure 1.1-3, within the EAB.
Based on PSAR section 2.1.2.2, the staff understands that Dow has total control over these
industrial basins.
In summary, the NRC staff evaluated the sufficiency of the PSAR information provided on
authority and control of the exclusion area of the proposed facility. The NRC staff finds that
NEER, as the operator of the LMGS, will have absolute authority on all lands within the EAB
from the pre-operational testing through plant operation. The NRC staff also finds that there are
no public roads, rail roads, or waterways traversing the EAB and that Dow controls all
commercial activities within the EAB and prohibits agricultural use, hunting, and recreational
activities using Dow security personnel. Consequently, no arrangements for traffic control will be
needed within the EAB as there are no public roads. The NRC staff also finds from PSAR figure
2.1.2-1 that there are no residences within the EAB and from PSAR figure 1.1-3 that there is no
public access to nearby water bodies. Therefore, the NRC staff concludes that LME has
identified the authority to administer control of all activities within the EAB.
2.1.2.2 Conclusion
Based on the above, the NRC staff finds that PSAR sections 2.1.1 and 2.1.2 provide sufficient
information on the exclusion area authority and control for the proposed site. In addition, the
staff finds that application provides information that satisfies both acceptance criteria in DANU-
ISG-2022-02, section 2.2.2.2, specifically a description of the legal authority for all activities
within the designated exclusion area and a demonstration that the activities permitted within the
exclusion area pose no hazard to the facility. The NRC staff therefore finds that the exclusion
area control requirements or 10 CFR 100.21 and 10 CFR 100.3 are met.

    2.1.3 Population Distribution
2.1.3.1 Technical Evaluation
The NRC staff evaluated the sufficiency of demographic information and acceptability of the
selected site based on the existing and projected future population profile of the area
surrounding the site using guidance in DANU-ISG-2022-02. The NRC staff reviewed the PSAR
to identify the data sources used for population estimates and the methodology used to project
population growth for the planned operational life of the facility. A summary of the information
provided in the PSAR that was evaluated by the staff to determine the acceptability of the
estimated population distribution is below.

Resident Population


                                                                                                     3
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                      OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


PSAR section 2.1.3 states that LME estimated the current population distribution surrounding
the proposed LMGS site using the US Census Bureau 2020 decennial census data. PSAR
section 2.1.3.1.1 discusses the resident population within 5 mi, 10 mi, and 20 mi from the
proposed site. PSAR tables 2.1.3-2 and 2.1.3-3 provide the distribution of resident population up
to 50 mi from the proposed site. PSAR figures 2.1.3-2 through 2.1.3-12 plot the distribution of
total population comprising both the resident and the transient population within 50 mi of the
proposed site. The NRC staff finds the use of the latest 2020 US Census Bureau information on
population is acceptable because it is an authoritative source.
PSAR section 2.1.3.4 identifies the City of Victoria as the nearest population center with more
than 25,000 residents. PSAR table 2.1.3-8 shows the population of the City of Victoria was
65,534 in 2020 and is expected to grow steadily. The NRC staff confirmed that the City of
Victoria is the nearest population center to the site. As this city has a population greater than
25,000 and is more than one and one-third distance times the distance from the reactor to the
outer boundary of the LPZ, this city satisfies the definition of the population center in 10 CFR
100.3 and 100.11(a)(3).
Transient Population
The estimated transient population near the proposed site comes from several sources; for
example, major employers, regional airports, schools, medical facilities, lodging facilities, and
recreational areas. The applicant assumed that all users of these facilities would be transient
visitors. The nearest transient population is at the L&W Frazier RV Park, approximately 0.6 mi
from the LPZ and EPZ boundaries. PSAR section 2.1.3.2.1 discusses information on visitors
developed from corporate and government websites, federal databases, tourism sites, and
records of aggregators of service providers. PSAR table 2.1.3-5 lists the estimated transient
population in 2020 within 20 mi of the proposed site. Estimates of the raw transient population
were weighted by the length of time each population group is expected to be in this area.
LME discussed in PSAR section 2.1.3.2.2 fifteen major recreational areas and 194 events and
attractions with large venues within 20 to 50 mi from the proposed site that generally draw large
numbers of visitors to the region. PSAR table 2.1.3-6 lists the known facilities attracting large
number visitors to this region. LME did not add this estimated transient population to the
estimated resident population. Transient population was projected using the same approach as
the resident population estimates for future years as discussed below.
The NRC staff finds that LME has used appropriate publicly available information to estimate
the current and future transient populations associated with the regional airports, major
employers, schools, medical facilities, lodging facilities, and recreational areas. The NRC staff
finds that assuming that all users of certain facilities within 20 mi of the proposed are transient
populations is a conservative assumption as many users of these facilities may also be counted
as residents. The NRC staff further finds that not adding visitors to major recreational areas and
events between 20 and 50 mi from the proposed site to the resident population is a reasonable
assumption as this transient population is at a significant distance, more than 20 mi from the
proposed site, and these visitors would be in this region for a limited period of time.
Population Density
In PSAR section 2.1.3.5, LME describes the population density within 20 mi surrounding the
proposed facility. LME provided the estimated population density in PSAR table 2.1.3-7. PSAR

                                                                                                    4
                     OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                     OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


figure 2.1.3-14 compares the projected population density, given in number of persons per
square mile (ppsm), with the guidance in RG 4.7, “General Site Suitability Criteria for Nuclear
Power Reactors,” which recommends that the projected population density should not exceed
500 ppsm at the time of initial site approval and for 5 years thereafter. Based on PSAR figure
2.13-14, LME concluded that the projected population density is less than that specified in the
regulatory guidance until the end of the operational life of the proposed facility. The nearest
transient population is at the L&W Frazier RV Park, approximately 0.6 mi from the LPZ and EPZ
boundaries. Estimated raw transient populations were weighted based on the length of time
each population group was expected to be within 20 mi of the proposed site.
PSAR figure 2.1.13-14 plots the estimated population density (number of persons per square
mile) against a 20 mi radial distance from the proposed site. The staff finds that the estimated
cumulative population density is less than 500 ppsm until 2070, which is consistent with the
guidelines specified in RG 4.7. Therefore, the NRC staff concludes that the proposed reactor
facility will be located away from densely populated centers.
Population Growth

Population distribution surrounding the proposed site was estimated for the years 2023, 2030,
2035, 2040, 2050, 2060, and 2070 using the county population projection dataset and the
methodology from the Texas Demographic Center under the Institute of Demographic and
Socioeconomic Research at the University of Texas at San Antonio. The annual population
growth rates of the nearby counties were estimated using the information from the Census
Bureau for years 2000 and 2020. Using this information, populations were projected for the 14
counties from a circle of 0.5 mi to concentric circles up to 50 mi from the site boundary. As
shown in PSAR figures 2.1.3-1 and 2.1.3-2 and tables 2.1.3-1 and 2.1.3-2, population is
estimated in concentric distance bands and in sixteen 22.5-degree wedge-shaped sectors.
The NRC staff finds that LME has used an acceptable methodology for the projected population
for the planned operational life of the facility. The projected annual population growth rates are
based on the 2000 and 2020 US Census Bureau and the population was projected county-wise
using information and methodology from the Texas Demographic Center, which is an
authoritative source.
Combined resident and transient population within 20 mi of the proposed site is shown in PSAR
figures 2.1.3-3 through 2.1.3-7 for years 2020, 2023, 2030, 2035, and 2070. The NRC staff finds
that LME has used the latest 2020 US Census data and projected the population data for future
years using appropriate methods. Projected population information was presented for the year
of facility approval and throughout the requested operating period of the proposed facility.
PSAR figure 2.1.3-13 shows the EAB and LPZ segments with a calculated population of 1
resident although no resident or transient population exists within these areas. This is a result of
the methodology used to project the population in each of the 22.5-degree segments. Based on
this information, the NRC staff concludes that LME can take protective measures for the
population within the LPZ.
2.1.3.2 Conclusion
Based on the above, the NRC staff finds that PSAR section 2.1.3 provides sufficient information
to describe the population distribution around the proposed site consistent with the guidance in
DANU-ISG-2022-02. The NRC staff finds that the applicant has appropriately estimated both the

                                                                                                   5
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                     OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


resident and transient populations for the expected operating life of the facility. Additionally, the
NRC staff find that the population density surrounding the proposed site is consistent with RG
1.47. Therefore, the NRC staff finds that the applicant provided sufficient information in the
PSAR to meet 10 CFR 100.3 and 10 CFR 100.21(a), (b), and (h).
  2.1.4   Conclusion

Based on its review, the NRC staff determined that the geographical and demographical
information provided in the PSAR is sufficiently detailed and accurate to support assessments of
the potential radiological impact on the public resulting from siting and operation of the proposed
LMGS facility, including analyses (e.g., dose calculations) presented in other PSAR chapters.
The NRC staff also finds that the geographic and demographic characteristics of the LMGS site
do not render the site unsuitable for operation of the LMGS facility, as the site is located in a low
population zone. The staff also finds that the information provided meets the applicable
acceptance criteria of DANU-ISG-2022-02, section 2.2. Accordingly, the staff determined that
the applicant meets the requirements in 10 CFR 50.34(a)(1)(ii), 10 CFR 100.3, and 10 CFR
100.21.
2.2   Nearby Industrial, Transportation, and Military Facilities
This section of the SE identifies, locates, and describes present and projected facilities and
transportation routes in the vicinity of the LMGS site. The facilities and transportation routes are
then evaluated to determine the effects of potential accidents in the vicinity of the LMGS site
and whether hazards due to the facilities and transportation routes need to be considered
design-basis events for plant design. Parameters used as the basis for the evaluations are
provided.

LME listed the industrial facilities within 5 mi of the proposed site in PSAR section 2.2.1. In
addition, LME described in PSAR section 2.2.2 the potential hazardous materials that are either
manufactured or stored at these facilities or transported using nearby transportation routes.
PSAR section 2.2.3 describes the analyses conducted and results obtained on whether any of
these external human-induced hazards can become a design-basis hazard to the proposed
facility. The NRC staff reviewed the description of the facilities and the analyses conducted to
determine whether LME used appropriate methods and analyses to screen out each potential
hazard. LME analyzed the following accident categories associated with nearby facilities and
transportation routes to identify any design-basis hazards: (1) aircraft crashes, (2) explosion
(detonation) from immediate ignition, (3) explosion (deflagration) from delayed ignition of vapor
cloud, (4) fires, and (5) toxic chemicals.

  2.2.1   Aircraft Crash Hazard

The NRC staff reviewed, following section 3.5.1.6 of NUREG-0800, LME’s assessment of
potential hazards from aircraft flying nearby to assess whether aircraft crashes onto the
proposed facility can be identified as a design-basis hazard.

2.2.1.1 Technical Evaluation
LME described the potential aircraft crash hazard at the proposed facility in PSAR section
2.2.2.7. The NRC staff reviewed the discussion provided in PSAR section 2.2.2.7 using
guidance in section 3.5.1.6 of NUREG–0800 (NRC, 2007). Additionally, the NRC staff used the
guidance given in the DOE Standard DOE–STD–3014–2006 (DOE, 2006) in this review. The
methodology in the DOE standard is consistent with NUREG-0800 and provides updated
information to perform aircraft crash analysis. The NRC staff also audited LME’s calculation
document “Aircraft Hazard Evaluation,” XE-C-ME-022, Rev. 1, 2024, by Sargent & Lundy to
confirm that the calculations support the information presented in the PSAR.

Nearby Airports

                                                                                                    7

                     OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


LME listed nearby airports to the proposed site in PSAR table 2.2-8. This table also provides the
distance to each airport from the proposed site and annual number of operations (take-offs and
landings). PSAR figure 2.2-5 shows locations of these airports with respect to the proposed site.
Based on information in PSAR table 2.2-8, only Whatley Flying Service (8TA1) is within 5 mi of
the proposed site and only aircraft used for occasional crop dusting (i.e., less than 25 times in a
year) use this airfield.

In PSAR section 2.2.2.7, LME identified two private airports within 10 mi of the proposed site:
Green Lake Ranch (69TX) and Tanners (9TE4). PSAR table 2.2-8 shows no operations taking
place at the Green Lake Ranch airport. Only general aviation aircraft use Tanners airport with
2,200 operations annually. Calhoun County Airport (PKV) is the only public airport within 10 mi
from the proposed site. Other public airports, such as Sterling airport (10XA), Victoria Regional
Airport (VCT), William P. Hobby Airport (HOU), and George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH)
are beyond 10 mi from the proposed site.

LME used the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) operational information to determine the
annual number of operations at these airports. LME screened out all airports, except Watley
Flying Service based on the number of annual operations and proximity to the proposed site.
The staff accepts LME’s screening of airports based on information in PSAR table 2.2-8, which
indicates that all airports listed have annual flight operations lower than that needed to pose a
credible hazard to the proposed facility based on the proximity criterion 1.A of section 3.5.1.6 of
NUREG–0800. In addition, the NRC staff concludes that because of the limited number of
annual operations of the crop duster aircraft using the Whatley Flying Service airport as well as
their flight elevation close to the ground, these aircraft do not pose a credible hazard to the
proposed facility.

Nearby Airways

PSAR figure 2.2-5 shows the Federal airways near the proposed site. In PSAR section
2.2.2.7.2, LME discussed hazards to the proposed facility from aircraft crashes while transiting
nearby Federal airways. LME listed two low-altitude Victor Airways, V13–V407 and V20–V70,
and one Jet Route J22–J29, near the proposed site. The centerline of the Victor Airway V13–
V407 is approximately 1 mi from the proposed site boundary; the centerline of the Victor Airway
V20–V70 is approximately 7.3 mi from the proposed site boundary; and the centerline of the Jet
Route J22–J29 is approximately 4.6 mi from the proposed site boundary. In addition, the military
airway VR–151 is more than 10 mi away from the proposed site. LME concluded that the
airways V13–V407 and J22–J29 do not satisfy the proximity criterion 1.C of section 3.5.1.6 of
NUREG–0800. Consequently, and consistent with the guidance in NUREG-0800, LME
conducted a detailed analysis of aircraft crash hazard to the proposed facility and the NRC
staff’s evaluation is below.

Annual Crash Frequency

LME used the DOE Standard DOE-STD-3014-2006 (DOE, 2006) to estimate the annual crash
frequency from aircraft. The NRC staff finds that the method presented in the DOE standard has
been used in several licensing proceedings of reactor facilities.


                                                                                                    8
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                     OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


As the proposed site is not close to any of the DOE facilities listed in DOE (2006), LME used the
parameter values of “Average CONUS” (continental United States) to estimate the annual crash
frequency from flights by all types of aircraft (i.e., general aviation, air carrier, air taxi, large
military, and small military) transiting these airways. LME estimated the annual crash frequency
to the proposed facility to be 2.97 × 10−6 crashes from all types of aircraft flying these airways,
as stated in PSAR section 2.2.2.7.2. Additionally, a major portion of the total aircraft crash
hazard, 2.85 × 10−6 crashes per year, is from general aviation aircraft on these airways, as
discussed in PSAR section 2.2.2.7. Therefore, based on the above discussion the NRC staff
finds that aircraft flying in the vicinity would pose a credible hazard to the proposed facility and
would need to be accounted for in designing the SR and certain NSRST SSCs at the proposed
facility.

LME recognizes this in PSAR section 2.2.2.7.2 and commits to performing a risk-informed
assessment of accidental aircraft impact hazards in accordance with the Non-LWR PRA
Standard (ASME, 2021) and NEI 18-04 (NEI, 2019) and providing it with the OL application.
LME did not address aircraft impact as a design basis hazard in PSAR section 6.1.1 at the CP
stage because of their expectation that it would be screened out with the more detailed analysis
at the OL application. Based on the level of conservatism in the data used for the analysis, NRC
staff agrees and determined that this is consistent with the guidance in NEI 21-07 which
indicates that the design basis hazard information provided in the PSAR should be sufficient to
support demonstrating the viability of the design. RG 1.253, Appendix A also indicates that
external hazards PRAs are not required to meet the requirements of a minimally acceptable
PRA at the CP stage.

If the risk-informed assessment of accidental aircraft impact hazards performed for the OL
application shows aircraft impact does not screen out and is a design basis event, it will need to
be addressed in the design and safety analysis to show that safety-significant SSCs are
designed to withstand the event or that the dose consequence is acceptable. The NRC staff
determined that this may also be a viable path based on the robustness of the reactor shield
structure and spent fuel intermediate storage structure.

2.2.1.2 Conclusions
The NRC staff finds that the estimated annual crash hazard has several conservative
assumptions. For example, the crash rate for each aircraft type comes from the DOE standard.
The aircraft crash rates in this standard were derived from actual aircraft crashes that occurred
before 1998. Advanced design of current aircraft with better training and other improvements in
the aviation industry make the current fleet of aircraft less crash prone reducing the crash rate
(number of crashes per mile of flight). In addition, the crash rates used were derived from
crashes that did not take place near the proposed facility. All non-airport crashes in the lower 48
states were used to derive the crash rates in the DOE standard. Therefore, the crash rate
includes crashes from areas that are crash prone, for example, areas with much higher flight
density than South Texas.

Based on the level of conservatism in the current screening analysis and the robustness in the
preliminary design, NRC staff determined that sufficient information was provided in the PSAR
to demonstrate viable paths for addressing aircraft impact at the OL stage.

  2.2.2    Description of Nearby Facilities and Transportation Routes

2.2.2.1 Technical Evaluation
The NRC staff reviewed the application to determine that that LME sufficiently evaluated
potential hazards associated with nearby transportation routes, industrial and military facilities,
and civilian and military airports to meet 10 CFR 100.20(b) and 10 CFR 100.21(e). PSAR tables
2.2-3 through 2.2-7 list the explosive and toxic chemicals that are transported by trucks,
pipelines, railcars, and barges near the proposed site. The NRC staff reviewed the PSAR to
determine that the descriptions and characteristics of nearby facilities, highways, railroads,
pipelines, and waterways were included in the application. A summary of the information
provided in the PSAR that allowed the staff to conclude that the application gives a complete
and current overview of the facilities, activities, and materials located in or transported through
the vicinity of the proposed site, as discussed in DANU-ISG-2022-02, is below.

Nearby Facilities

PSAR table 2.2-1 lists major projects of the Dow SDO, Braskem, Calhoun Chemical, and
INEOS Nitriles chemical plants located near the proposed site. Dow SDO is adjacent (within
0.5 mi) to the proposed site and is located just south of Texas highway TX-35 along TX-185, as
stated in PSAR section 2.2.2.2.1. Dow SDO manufactures polyethylene, glycols, and oxide
derivatives. PSAR table 2.2-2 lists the chemicals stored or manufactured at this facility along
with their lower explosive limit (LEL) and toxicity limit. Dow SDO uses a barge dock on the

potential to generate an overpressure exceeding 1 pound per square inch differential (psid) at

LME assessed whether a particular event at a facility would generate an overpressure
damaging to safety-related structures at the proposed facility in two ways. Following RG 1.91, if
the estimated overpressure of 1 psid occurs at a distance smaller than that between the source
location (location of availability or release) and NI area of the proposed facility, the structures
would be safe. Alternatively, if the concentration of a chemical estimated at the NI location of the
proposed facility is less than its lower explosive limit (LEL) value, there will not be an explosion

to demonstrate that the event is rare, with a frequency of occurrence below 1 × 10−6 annually.

   2.2.4 Explosion (Deflagration) from Delayed Ignition of Vapor Clouds
Flammable materials may be stored and/or transported as gas or liquid under pressure near the
proposed site. Accidental release of the lighter than air flammable materials to the atmosphere
can develop a vapor cloud (plume of chemicals floating in the air), which may travel toward the
LMGS nuclear island (NI) under prevailing atmospheric conditions. Structures in the NI area of
the proposed facility may provide some confinement to the vapor cloud and may also provide
the ignition source(s) for the plume to ignite. Reactors and other buildings on the NI may also
provide the necessary congestion in the propagation path of the flame propagation in the vapor
cloud to transition from a deflagration (rapid burning) event to a detonation (flame speed higher
than the speed of sound) event. A typically gaseous chemical stored as a compressed liquid
could flash to vapor isoentropically and the chemicals that do not flash to vapor would form a
pool near the point of release, similar to chemicals that are liquid at standard conditions. The
liquid from the pool can evaporate with time forming a vapor cloud.

The vapor cloud of a released flammable chemical can ignite after encountering an ignition
source (delayed ignition) and explode (vapor cloud explosion (VCE)), if sufficient quantity of the
material in the vapor cloud is within its flammable/explosive range, that is, between the lower
explosive limit (LEL) and the upper explosive limit (UEL). The vapor cloud may burn as a flash
fire depending on the ignition source. If a pipeline carrying pressurized flammable material
ruptures, the pressurized chemical can be released to the atmosphere with large momentum
(like a jet). A jet fire may ensue near the release point of the chemical. The plume of vapor can
also burn as a flash fire upon encountering an ignition source. A BLEVE event can take place if
a tank of flammable material is exposed to fire. Blast overpressure can develop from a VCE and
a BLEVE. A flash fire and a jet fire can damage nearby structures through thermal radiation
although a flash fire typically has low heat load to cause any significant damage. A BLEVE can
also produce a thermal flux causing damage to nearby structures.

LME assessed the damaging effects from potential VCEs, jet fires, and BLEVEs of the
flammable chemicals stored at nearby facilities and/or transported on nearby transportation
